{{Use mdy dates|date=September 2020}}
{{short description|Polish-American aerodynamicist}}
'''Saul Kaplun''' (July 3, 1924<ref name=MySon>{{cite book | title=My son Saul | via=www.amazon.com| date=January 1965| publisher=Shengold Publishers| url=https://www.amazon.com/My-son-Saul-1924-February-memoriam/dp/B0007FM6VO | access-date=July 22, 2020}}</ref> Lwów,<ref name=CalLib>{{cite web |url=http://calteches.library.caltech.edu/237/1/saul.pdf |title=Bio |website= calteches.library.caltech.edu|access-date=July 22, 2020}}</ref> Poland now [[Lviv]], Ukraine – February 13, 1964,<ref name=MySon/> [[Pasadena, California]], U.S.A.) was a Polish-American aerodynamicist<ref name=CalLib/> at the [[California Institute of Technology]] (Caltech).

==Family==
Kaplun was the only child<ref name=BentLy>{{Cite web|url=https://digital.bentley.umich.edu/djnews/djn.1965.12.03.001/10|title=December 03, 1965 – Image 10|website=The Detroit Jewish News Digital Archives}}</ref> of Jewish immigrants from Poland, Morris J. Kaplun (February 12, 1888<ref name=CrtIi>{{cite web |url=https://www.crt-ii.org/_awards/_apdfs/Kaplun_M.J.pdf |title= Litigation documents |website= www.crt-ii.org|access-date=July 22, 2020}}</ref> Kamenetz-Podolsk,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/Kamyanets_Podilskyy1/kam089.html|title=Kamyanets Podilskyy, Ukraine (Pages 89–102)|website=www.jewishgen.org}}</ref> Ukraine – ?), a textile businessman and industrialist<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.jta.org/1977/03/04/archive/4-receive-kaplun-prizes|title=4 Receive Kaplun Prizes|date=March 4, 1977}}</ref>
and a prominent [[Zionist]] philanthropist<ref>{{cite book | title=Profile | via=www.amazon.com | date=January 1968 | publisher=Shengold Publishers | url=https://www.amazon.com/Profile-purposeful-living-Morris-Kaplun/dp/B0006BV2PU | access-date=July 22, 2020}}</ref> beginning in the 1930s,<ref name=KapFund>{{Cite web|url=https://www.kaplunfoundation.org/|title=Kaplun Foundation|website=Kaplun Foundation}}</ref> and Betty (Bettina) Kaplun<ref name=CrtIi/> (? – 1963).<ref name=BentLy/> Saul and his parents, who were refugees from [[Nazi]] persecution,<ref name=KapFund/> lived in Lwów until 1939, when they fled Poland;<ref name=CrtIi/> they immigrated to New York shortly before [[World War II]].<ref name=BentLy/> He became a [[naturalized]] American citizen in 1944 and served in the [[United States Navy]] from 1944 to 1946.<ref name=CalLib/>

Upon his death at age 39 of a heart attack, three months after his mother's death,<ref name=BentLy/> Saul Kaplun left behind a grieving father,<ref name=MySon/> who sought to perpetuate his son's memory by endowing several educational projects in Israel and the United States.

At the dedication ceremony of one of the institutions he funded, at [[Tel Aviv University]],<ref name=TLV>{{Cite web|url=https://www.jta.org/1964/10/20/archive/tel-aviv-university-to-get-new-facility-named-after-dr-saul-kaplun|title=Tel Aviv University to Get New Facility Named After Dr. Saul Kaplun|date=October 20, 1964}}</ref> Morris Kaplun himself "learned for the first time just how important a man [his son] was in his field. The late Dr. Saul Kaplun… left behind 'a roomful of manuscripts' which Prof. [[Paco Lagerstrom]], of the California Institute of Technology, who spoke at the dedication, said contained 'a wealth of scientific ideas far outweighing his published work'."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://newspapers.library.in.gov/cgi-bin/indiana?a=d&d=JPOST19660610-01.1.11&e=-------en-20--1--txt-txIN------|title=Jewish Post 10 June 1966 — Hoosier State Chronicles: Indiana's Digital Historic Newspaper Program|website=newspapers.library.in.gov}}</ref>

==Career==
Saul Kaplun received his PhD in 1954 under the advisorship of Paco Lagerstrom at the California Institute of Technology<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=78828|title=Saul Kaplun - the Mathematics Genealogy Project}}</ref> with his thesis dissertation ''The role of [[coordinate systems]] in [[boundary layer theory]]''.<ref>{{Cite thesis|url=https://thesis.library.caltech.edu/4738/|doi = 10.7907/9QZM-8W36|year = 1954|last1 = Kaplun|first1 = Saul|title = The role of coordinate systems in boundary layer theory|publisher = California Institute of Technology|type = phd}}</ref> Kaplun and Lagerstrom later collaborated on and published an article together<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Asymptotic Expansions of Navier-Stokes Solutions for Small Reynolds Numbers|author1=Kaplun, Saul|author2=Lagerstrom, P. A.|year=1957|journal=Journal of Mathematics and Mechanics|volume=6|issue=5|pages=585–593|jstor = 24900496}}</ref> and Lagerstrom edited Kaplun's papers for publication as a [[monograph]] after the latter's death.<ref name="sciencedirect.com">{{Cite book|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/9780123955746/fluid-mechanics-and-singular-perturbations|title=Fluid Mechanics and Singular Perturbations |publisher=Elsevier|isbn=9780123955746 }}</ref>

Kaplun spent his entire academic career, a total of 20 years, at Caltech and received four degrees there.<ref name=CalLib/> He became a research fellow in aeronautics upon completing his PhD in 1954 and was a senior [[research fellow]] in aeronautics on the Caltech faculty from 1957 until his death.<ref name=CalLib/>

At a memorial ceremony at Caltech held that same year, Dr. [[Clark Blanchard Millikan]], Caltech professor of aeronautics, stated, "Saul Kaplun's very special hallmark as a scientist was his unusual intuition. He lived with a problem till he 'saw' the solution. This enabled him to understand the essence of some fundamental problems but also made it difficult for others to understand his work. His work could in general not be explained by [[discursive reasoning]]; one had to make an effort to share his intuitive thinking."<ref name=CalLib/>

In the ceremony, Millikan also noted that "Saul Kaplun's work played a decisive role in the development of applied mathematics at the California Institute."<ref name=CalLib/>
Caltech President [[Lee Alvin DuBridge]] eulogized at the same ceremony, "Saul Kaplun had a brilliant analytical and creative mind and made many profound and original contributions to the theory of [[fluid mechanics]]. He was an applied mathematician of extraordinary ability and had already won wide and admiring recognition for his work."<ref name=CalLib/>

==Publications==
Dr. Millikan stated at the 1964 Caltech ceremony, "Few publications bear his name as author… however, in very many publications by others the author expresses his thanks to Saul Kaplun for having contributed some fundamental ideas to the work, or states that he has used methods due to Kaplun. By now his work has won world-wide recognition among specialists."<ref name=CalLib/>

After Kaplun's untimely death, his published papers and much of his unpublished work were edited by his former PhD advisor, Lagerstrom, and by [[Louis Norberg Howard]] of MIT and Ching-shi Liu of Caltech and were published in 1967 in book form under the title ''Fluid Mechanics and [[Singular Perturbation]], a Collection of Papers by Saul Kaplun''.<ref name="sciencedirect.com"/>

Kaplun's work has been cited and extolled by colleagues and authors in the field. [[Robert Edmund O'Malley]] wrote, "The work of Kaplun and Lagerstrom at Caltech in the 1950s was especially important to the development of matched expansions and its applications to fluid mechanics."<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://www.springer.com/gp/book/9783319119236|title=Historical Developments in Singular Perturbations|first=Robert E.|last=O'Malley|date=July 22, 2014|publisher=Springer International Publishing|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-11924-3|isbn=978-3-319-11923-6|via=www.springer.com}}</ref>

Sunil Datta wrote, "Singular perturbation method… It was left to the genius of Saul Kaplun (1957) to recognize the analogy between the theory of flow at small Reynolds number and boundary layer theory and to apply to it the singular perturbation method."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://bharataganitaparisad.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/ch3-68-3.pdf |title= Mathematics and Fluid Mechanics|date=2018 |website=bharataganitaparisad.com |access-date=July 22, 2020}}</ref>

==Legacy==
[[File:Kaplun building Racah Institute Givat Ram 2010.JPG|thumb|Kaplun building Hebrew University]]
[[File:אוניברסיטת תל אביב בנין לחקר ביולוגיה.jpg|thumb|Science Faculty Tel Aviv University including Kaplun Building]]
Morris Kaplun's philanthropy included funding of the Saul Kaplun Institute of Applied Mathematics and Space Physics at Tel Aviv University, Israel,<ref name=TLV/><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://jpress.org.il/olive/apa/nli_heb/SharedView.Article.aspx?href=DAV/1966/02/18&id=Ar01003|title=נחנר המכון למתמטיקה. שימושית באזניברסיטת ת"א|website=jpress.org.il}}</ref> consecrated in February 1966, which was attended by Prof. Paco Lagerstrom and others; and of the Saul Kaplun Building for Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics at the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]] dedicated a month later in the presence of the university president, [[Eliahu Eilat]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.jta.org/1966/03/17/archive/saul-kaplun-300000-building-dedicated-at-hebrew-university|title=Saul Kaplun $300,000 Building Dedicated at Hebrew University|date=March 17, 1966}}</ref>

Morris Kaplun also established a memorial fellowship which funds graduate research in applied mathematics and is awarded in perpetuity in his son's name at Caltech.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cms.caltech.edu/academics/honors|title=Caltech Computing + Mathematical Sciences &#124; Honors and Awards|website=Caltech Computing + Mathematical Sciences}}</ref>

The father wrote a short book about his son: My Son Saul: Saul Kaplun, July 3, 1924 – February 13, 1964, in Memoriam, published in 1965.<ref name=MySon/>
